steps: Distance-time graph: gradient = speed; a flat line = a rest; use speed = distance ÷ time.
Speed-time graph: the area under the line = distance; the gradient = acceleration.
Split an area into a triangle (½ × base × height) plus a rectangle (base × height), then add.
Conversion graph: read up to the line, then across to the other axis. Always give units.
method_card.title: How to Interpret Real-Life Graphs
method_card.content:
Real-life graphs show how one quantity changes with another. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed, a flat line is a rest, and the total distance is the final height. Speed = distance ÷ time.

On a speed-time graph the area under the line is the distance travelled, and the gradient is the acceleration (change in speed ÷ time). Break the area into a triangle for any speeding up or slowing down and a rectangle for constant speed, then add them.

A conversion graph swaps units: read up to the line, then across. Always write the units in your answer.
method_card.example:
A car accelerates from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s, then holds 20 m/s for 10 s. Find the distance.

Triangle: ½ × 5 × 20 = 50 m. Rectangle: 10 × 20 = 200 m. Total = 250 m.

steps: A full speed-time journey has three areas: a triangle for speeding up, a rectangle for the steady middle, and a triangle for slowing down. Find each and add for the total distance.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. On a distance-time graph, include every rest in the total time.
Acceleration = change in speed ÷ time, the gradient of a speed-time line.

example.question: A speed-time graph: 0 to 12 m/s in 3 s, hold 12 m/s for 5 s, slow to 0 in 2 s. Find the distance.

steps: Speed = distance ÷ time. On a distance-time graph this is the steepness (gradient) of the line: read a distance off the up axis and the matching time off the across axis, then divide.
A flat line means a rest: the distance is not changing, so the speed is 0. The rest lasts from where the line goes flat to where it starts rising again.
The total distance is the highest value the line reaches, read at the very end of the journey.

steps: On a speed-time graph the distance is the area under the line. Split the shape into a triangle (for speeding up or slowing down) and a rectangle (for constant speed), then add the areas.
Triangle area = ½ × base × height; rectangle area = base × height. The base is a time, the height is a speed.
For acceleration, use the gradient: change in speed ÷ time. For a conversion graph, read up to the line then across to the other axis.
